stories.headline: SpaceX's AI unit now out-earns Starlink: $7.56B in Q3 and 200,000 GB300s coming online every month
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: you reposted Sawyer Merritt's full earnings rundown last night, and it's the clearest look yet at what a frontier AI compute business costs and earns.
body: SpaceX's Super Intelligence segment (formerly the AI segment) brought in $7.56 billion in the third quarter, up 830 percent year over year and 195 percent quarter over quarter, which makes it bigger than Connectivity's $5.25 billion for the first time. It also turned an operating profit of $431 million, after a $1.26 billion loss in Q2, and posted $4.95 billion of adjusted EBITDA. SI capex was $16.44 billion, about 84 percent of the company's $19.59 billion total, and SpaceX guided to $35 to $40 billion of capex in Q4. Cursor alone contributed $608 million of revenue between August 14 and September 30.

The hardware numbers are the part to sit with. Nameplate compute reached 1.7 GW, up from 1.4 GW in Q2 and 0.6 GW a year ago, with nearly 2 GW expected by the end of October and 2.5 to 3 GW by year end. SpaceX says it is bringing roughly 200,000 to 220,000 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs online per month, plans a 440,000 Vera Rubin training cluster by the end of Q2 2027, and Musk expects to add at least 10 GW in 2027. Newly deployed capacity is paying back in under 12 months at current pricing, and first functional test chips from the Austin research fab are targeted for May or June 2027. X News adds that NVIDIA shares rose over 2 percent after hours on the deployment plans.

stories.headline: Tesla and SpaceX boards form committees to study a merger after SpaceX's record $4.4B quarter
stories.why_read: The single biggest thread across your reposts and X News this morning, and Tesla reports its own quarter after the close today.
body: Tesla and SpaceX each created independent director committees on Tuesday to study a possible combination, following shareholder requests. On SpaceX's earnings call Musk called the idea a good one, pointing to overlap in AI, chips, robotics, and connectivity. X News notes that approval looks easier at SpaceX given Musk's voting control, while Tesla would need half of all outstanding shares, which hands retail holders real influence. No terms exist and nothing is guaranteed.

The backdrop is a blowout quarter: $14.58 billion in revenue, up 161 percent year over year, $4.40 billion of GAAP net income versus a $1.05 billion loss a year earlier, and about $90 billion of cash and securities. X News says SpaceX shares rose 7.67 percent to $159.72 while Tesla traded near $381.65, and retail investors are already swapping hypothetical exchange ratios of 1.67 to 1.92 SpaceX shares per Tesla share. Watch the lock-up expiration that starts October 22, which X News said could free up to 1.3 billion shares.

stories.headline: Grok Bot hits 800,000 paid weekly users, more than doubling in a month
stories.why_read: You reposted the number, and it is the product you're reading this paper through.
body: SpaceX disclosed that Grok Bot reached 800,000 paid weekly users in early October, more than double the prior month. X News adds that daily active users nearly tripled to 450,000 by mid-October and that Musk highlighted deeper engagement, with people coming back for complex, multi-step workflows. An enterprise rollout is expected within a few weeks, according to the earnings call highlights.

For context, an X News roundup from earlier in the beta described Grok Bot at 418,000 weekly users growing 24 percent week over week, with users building routines and specialist bots for email, invoices, and websites. The doubling also feeds directly into the SI segment's revenue line above.

stories.headline: Software factories: build, buy, or delegate to an always-on agent?
stories.why_read: Two of the five posts you reposted this morning are about this, and it's squarely your day job: developer platforms for thousands of engineers.
body: Zach Lloyd argues the point of a software factory is not full automation, at least not today. It is getting the most out of coding agents so a team ships the highest-quality, highest-impact software as quickly and efficiently as possible, and proving it by carefully measuring and tuning the factory, which he calls "factory engineering."

Josh Rosen lays out three routes. Build your own factory infrastructure around coding agents; buy a platform such as Warp, Factory, or Port; or delegate to an always-on agent like @bot as the factory. He says delegating is by far the easiest to set up and gets you coordination, ticket updates, and clarifying questions out of the box, but it lacks the defining feature of a factory: a system you can measure, iterate on, and continuously improve.

stories.headline: eMudhra's CA private keys were single bytes. One of them is the number 4
stories.why_read: Two eMudhra threads sit near the top of Hacker News, and this is the most jaw-dropping PKI failure in years, with a clean explanation of why.
body: Scott Helme recovered the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates from their public certificates in under a second. They are P-384 elliptic-curve keys that should be random 384-bit numbers, but each is 47 bytes of zeros followed by a single byte, so finding one means at most 255 point multiplications. The set is six TLS issuing CAs (DV, OV, and EV, two generations each) and two code-signing CAs created in April 2025, all cross-signed by Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root in May 2025.

A researcher reported the problem on Saturday, October 17. Chrome pushed a CRLSet block that evening and Firefox followed via OneCRL a few hours later; on Tuesday Mozilla announced it publicly and shipped an NSS update removing the eMudhra root, and Chrome confirmed the root is going in Chrome Root Store v43. As Ian Carroll put it in the thread, the keys are inherently weak and "the issue cannot be contained."

stories.headline: Ornith-1.5-122B lands under MIT with 0.845 on SWE-bench Verified
stories.why_read: A new open-weights coding model you can pull into Ollama with one command, aimed right at your open-source LLM interest.
body: The Ornith team released Ornith-1.5-122B on October 20 under the MIT license. X News reports scores of 0.845 on SWE-bench Verified and 0.813 on TerminalBench 2.1, which it says lead among open models of similar size.

It is on Hugging Face with deployment guides, on Ollama for local runs, and already has quantized builds for cards like the RTX PRO 6000. Early users are praising it as strong, fast, and efficient in one package, which is the trade-off most local-model builders actually care about.

stories.headline: NVIDIA's OpenShell: an open-source sandboxed runtime for enterprise agents
stories.why_read: Agent security is becoming platform plumbing, and this pairs NVIDIA's chips with exactly the kind of runtime your DevOps org will be asked to run.
body: Jensen Huang introduced the OpenShell Reference Architecture, an open-source secure runtime that runs AI agents in isolated sandboxes with strict policy enforcement on system calls and network access. It combines Vera Rubin systems for inference, Vera CPUs for agent management, and BlueField-4 DPUs for continuous monitoring, and supports enterprise infrastructure and operating systems from vendors like Canonical and Red Hat.

X News reports more than 100 partners, including Anthropic, AWS, Microsoft, and OpenAI, are integrating it to keep agents within defined boundaries while they reach files, tools, and private data. Huang's line: "AI capability and safety must advance together."

stories.headline: Starlink is now contracted on 12,000 aircraft, about a quarter of the fleet
stories.why_read: You reposted Gwynne Shotwell's line, and in-flight Wi-Fi is about to get a lot more consistent.
body: Gwynne Shotwell said Starlink is contracted with roughly 12,000 aircraft, nearly a quarter of the available commercial market, and that SpaceX has quadrupled aviation production since the start of the year and expects to double it again by year end. More than 3,800 aircraft were equipped as of September 30.

The rest of Connectivity was strong too: 13.6 million Starlink subscribers, up 89 percent, consumer ARPU up to $69 a month from $66, and Starlink Mobile above 22 million monthly users, up 37 percent quarter over quarter. SpaceX plans to activate its expanded U.S. mobile service in early 2028.

stories.headline: SpaceX guides to $33-37B of revenue in Q1 2027, and the Apple comparisons begin
stories.why_read: You reposted the CFO quote plus Jon Erlichman's revenue staircase and Phil Beisel's "catch Apple" math.
body: SpaceX CFO @BretWJ said the company now sees total revenue of $33 to $37 billion in Q1 2027, and it remains on track for a $100 billion annualized run rate by the end of 2026 based on December revenue. Jon Erlichman's staircase shows the trajectory: $10.4 billion in 2023, $14.0 billion in 2024, $18.7 billion in 2025, and $27.1 billion in just the first nine months of 2026.

Phil Beisel's back-of-envelope take is that SpaceX's compute business alone, at 13 GW of rentable capacity by the end of 2027 renting at $30 to $50 billion per GW, books out to $390 to $650 billion once built, against Apple's roughly $480 billion of 2026 revenue. Treat it as a bull case, not a forecast.

stories.headline: Musk: scaling AI compute is a power, memory, networking, cooling, and construction problem all at once
stories.why_read: It's the engineering reality behind the capex number, and you reposted a defense of that capex as smart spending.
body: Musk laid out on X that building giant AI systems means synchronizing power, memory, networking, cooling, and construction at speed, not just finding electricity. X News says SpaceX is even casting its own turbine blades to cut delays on the way from 1.7 GW today to 13 GW by late 2027, and others in the industry chimed in with transformer waits, labor shortages, and grid delays, citing the 122-day Colossus build in Memphis as the execution benchmark.

The bull argument you reposted from @TSLAFanMtl is simple payback math: if $10 of capex generates $10 a year and the asset keeps producing after year one, spending more is smart, even with borrowed money. SpaceX's own claim of sub-12-month payback on new compute is the number that has to hold.

stories.headline: Tesla reports Q3 after the close today; call at 5:30 p.m. ET
stories.why_read: Your Tesla follow is the obvious reason, and the merger committee news gives this call a brand-new first question.
body: Tesla already reported 486,532 Q3 deliveries, about 5 percent above estimates, along with 464,391 units produced and 13.7 GWh of energy storage deployed. X News says Wall Street expects revenue around $28 billion, roughly flat year over year, non-GAAP EPS of $0.45, and automotive gross margins near 17.9 percent.

The call is at 5:30 p.m. ET (4:30 p.m. CT) and should focus on profitability, energy, AI, and robotaxi updates. Traders note that management's tone usually moves the stock more than the numbers, and this time the SpaceX merger question will almost certainly come up.

stories.headline: Bare feet on Cybercab seats: the first robotaxi etiquette fight
stories.why_read: A lighter Cybercab story out of Austin, and a real question about shared driverless cars that nobody has solved yet.
body: Jeremy Judkins posted video of a relaxed ride in Tesla's two-seat Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or pedals and offers paid rides in Austin, with his bare feet on the seat. X News says the clip drew a wave of hygiene complaints, with some comparing robotaxis to public trains, while supporters praised turning traffic time into personal downtime.
Judkins shrugged off the criticism. The episode is a reminder that without a driver in the car, cleanliness and passenger behavior become a fleet-operations problem, not a social one.

stories.headline: Hutto, Texas weighs a three-Cybertruck police pilot
stories.why_read: It's right up the road from Austin, and you reposted it.
body: The Hutto City Council directed staff to compare costs for a three-vehicle test of Tesla Cybertrucks for the police department, after council member Jerrel Reynolds bought one in April and found fuel and maintenance costs low. He pointed to the Las Vegas Police Department, which has 10 Cybertrucks in its fleet, and suggested Hutto ask it for data.
Each Las Vegas police Cybertruck is expected to save about $9,500 a year in fuel and maintenance, per the post. Mayor Mike Snyder's verdict: "I think this is the future."

stories.headline: Waymo will launch driverless rides in Madrid in 2027
stories.why_read: The robotaxi race is going international, and this is the competitor benchmark for Tesla's Austin fleet.
body: Waymo said on October 20 that its fully autonomous ride-hailing service will launch in Madrid next year, its first city in Spain and second in the EU after Munich. Mapping starts soon with electric Jaguar I-PACE SUVs, followed by safety testing.

X News notes Waymo's U.S. record of more than 20 million paid trips, and that Madrid officials framed the move as a win for cleaner mobility, though traditional taxi operators may push back. Sign-ups for updates are open on Waymo's site.

stories.headline: Neuralink's Blindsight: first human implants in 6 to 12 months, Musk says
stories.why_read: Equal parts science and human-interest: restoring some sight to people blind from birth would be a genuine kindness amplifier.
body: Blindsight skips damaged eyes and stimulates the visual cortex directly. Musk says initial human implants will happen in the next 6 to 12 months, including for people blind from birth, with basic light perception as the first goal and later upgrades toward much higher resolution, infrared, and radar vision.
X News says the device has FDA breakthrough designation and one trial patient has already perceived simple stimuli. Reactions mix hope with skepticism about Neuralink's past timeline slips.

stories.headline: Canada picks Telesat Lightspeed over Starlink for Arctic military comms
stories.why_read: A sovereignty counterpoint to Starlink's record quarter.
body: Canada awarded Telesat a $2.3 billion contract in August to expand its Lightspeed constellation by 69 satellites for secure Arctic military communications, with service starting in 2028. Prime Minister Carney pointed to past Starlink disruptions tied to global conflicts as a key concern.
Supporters cheer the move toward technological sovereignty. Critics, per X News, note Telesat's limited near-term coverage, higher costs, and continued reliance on SpaceX for launches.

stories.headline: Inside Grok Bot: is the agent harness dead?
stories.why_read: You reposted the talk, and it's a builder's-eye view of why Grok Bot puts guardrails back that Cursor took out.
body: At AI Engineer New York, @jediahkatz of SpaceXAI explained why smarter models have let Cursor remove prompts and guardrails, and why Grok Bot is adding them back. The full talk is on YouTube.

Separately, Matt Palmer posted a tour of what's new in Grok Bot: new chat cards, speed, draft edits, email aliases, X DMs, tagging @bot, connectors, voice calls, notifications, invites and Android Assistant, plus access lists, unread, routines, and sign-in. His summary: "This team ships!"

stories.headline: Ask your agent for a statechart, then hunt bugs with TLA+
stories.why_read: A practical agent workflow you reposted, with formal methods sneaking back into everyday coding.
body: Lauren (@poteto) describes asking a coding agent to draw a statechart of a user flow, then running a /create-formal-verification-skill built with pstack to find bugs through something like TLA+.
The payoff she describes: you understand both your code and how the user flow should work, and fix issues users would otherwise hit. The post has more than 3,200 likes.

stories.headline: Energon swaps Mermaid.js for kepano's pele and gets ~520x faster diagrams
stories.why_read: You reposted it this morning, and it's from the Obsidian creator, which matters for your vault-heavy workflow.
body: Energon 1.15.1 now renders diagrams with pele, a project from @kepano that serves as a drop-in replacement for mermaid.js. Trevin Chow says in his tests it runs about 520x faster and loads 7x less JavaScript per diagram.
Both pele.run and getenergon.com are linked from the post if you want to try it.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse share links exposed private chats; researchers found 6,800 with one query
stories.why_read: An AI-agent privacy failure on the HN front page, from the product Zuckerberg called built for privacy.
body: Researchers at security firm Claroc enumerated 6,800 conversation-share links that Muse users had created, and after opening a few hundred found material clearly not meant to be public: confidential executive-search notes, an internal revenue review, a loan application, a bank fraud alert with a partial account number, and a full-year staff vacation calendar. "It took one query," they wrote.

Ars Technica reports that Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it reviews the design. The lesson is old but keeps recurring: an unguessable URL is only private if it is actually unguessable and undiscoverable.

stories.headline: Anthropic: use models to shrink reachable code, not just find bugs
stories.why_read: A defensive security idea that fits platform engineering: cut what a deployment exposes and every unknown bug gets less dangerous.
body: Anthropic's Chris Rohlf previews research on automated attack surface analysis and reduction: using Claude to map which code is reachable, then removing or restricting anything a given deployment doesn't need to expose.

The argument is that bug-by-bug fixing scales poorly, because fixing one critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the ones that remain. Reducing reachability lowers the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including ones under active exploitation, without ever finding them.

stories.headline: 333 hijacked Tor exit nodes tried to MITM SSH. One user got them pulled
stories.why_read: A great systems war story, and a reminder to never ignore that REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED warning.
body: On October 2, 333 infected Tor exit relays, roughly 10 percent of Tor's ~3,000 exits, began a coordinated campaign. The attackers had quietly installed the Ebury 1.8.3 OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer two months earlier, then blocked ports so their exits carried only unencrypted mail traffic while redirecting SSH on port 22 to one of 12 interception servers.
The author hit the host-key-changed warning on a Friday morning, investigated, and got more than 300 of the nodes removed. The post walks through the detection.

stories.headline: Cloudflare and VoidZero's tsrs: TypeScript ported to Rust, up to 8x faster
stories.why_read: Faster type-checking is a direct dev-productivity win for large monorepos, and this one is being done with the TypeScript team, not against it.
body: Cloudflare and VoidZero, working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com, are building tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler incubated in the Oxc toolchain and developed in close collaboration with the TypeScript team. They stress it is not a fork: the TypeScript team stays in control of the language.

Early benchmarks show tsrs up to 8x faster with about 70 percent less memory than TypeScript 7.0 at the same number of type-check workers, and some optimizations have already been upstreamed into TypeScript 7.1 beta, itself up to 2.5x faster than 7.0. An experimental build is on npm as tsrs.

stories.headline: Google open-sources TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs
stories.why_read: PyTorch on TPUs without the usual detour, a meaningful crack in the CUDA-default world.
body: TorchTPU provides a PyTorch backend for Google's TPUs, with custom ATen kernels, a compilation cache for XLA computations, torch.compile() integration for graph mode, and support for data and tensor parallelism. It ships examples for Llama, Qwen, ResNet, DLRM, minGPT, and UNet.
Version 0.2.0 is on PyPI for Python 3.11 and later, and the docs include interactive Marimo notebooks that run on a TPU VM; a v6e instance is the easiest start. It is at 349 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Mistral's Voxtral 3: speech models plus a voice-agent SDK in 50+ languages
stories.why_read: A big HN thread, and part of a broader shift toward voice agents that can actually take actions.
body: Voxtral 3 is a new family of speech-to-text and text-to-speech models plus a voice agent SDK that puts listening, reasoning, tool calling, and speaking into one real-time streaming pipeline, aimed at contact centers, service desks, assistants, and hands-free copilots. It is available through Mistral's EU-hosted API or self-deployment.

X News reports Voxtral 3 tops speech-to-text leaderboards at 2.1 percent error, and that Gradium open-sourced its Phonon TTS models the same day at 31M and 40M parameters, small enough to fit in 64MB for offline use on phones and a Raspberry Pi.

stories.headline: First patient treated with AI-designed bacteriophages
stories.why_read: AI meets biology in a real clinic, a good science story with a human at the center.
body: Radical Numerics used its Omnii-1 model to design bacteriophages targeting a patient's drug-resistant E. coli infection. After lab tests showed the phages killed the bacteria, doctors gave the therapy through a compassionate-use pathway when other options had failed, which X News calls the first clinical use of AI-generated phages in a human.
The company did not share outcomes, to protect the patient's privacy, and says one case shows feasibility but larger studies are needed on safety and efficacy.

stories.headline: In Hilbert space, all things are quantumly possible
stories.why_read: Pure physics from Quanta, on the HN front page, for the Physics/Chem/Math corner of your pinned post.
body: Charlie Wood explains why quantum mechanics asks you to stop picturing objects whizzing through ordinary space and instead track a vector in an abstract possibility space. As Perimeter Institute physicist Lucien Hardy puts it, these arrows are "really pointing in a direction in a possibility space."
That arena is Hilbert space, the stage on which every quantum prediction plays out. The piece is a friendly tour of why the math works the way it does.

stories.headline: UNEP: the Paris 1.5C goal is no longer viable
stories.why_read: The energy-transition backdrop to all that new data-center power, and a top HN debate today.
body: The UN Environment Programme's 2026 Emissions Gap Report, titled The Point of Return, says the chance to hold warming to 1.5C with no or limited overshoot has been lost. The new target is to stay below 2C and bring temperatures back down to 1.5C by the end of the century.

That would require cutting global greenhouse gas emissions 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035, and 69 percent by 2040 relative to 2025, far beyond current national commitments even if fully implemented.

stories.headline: Chiricahua becomes America's 64th national park
stories.why_read: You reposted it last night: a "Wonderland of Rocks" in Arizona, and a nice break from earnings.
body: The Interior Department announced that Chiricahua is officially the 64th U.S. national park, nicknamed the "Wonderland of Rocks." Its post called the new park "rock solid."
The announcement has more than 24,000 likes, one of the warmest reactions to anything on your timeline this week.

stories.headline: Beacon open-sources shared memory across 20+ coding agents
stories.why_read: If you bounce between coding agents, losing context on every switch is the tax this tries to remove.
body: Asymptote Labs launched Beacon on October 20 alongside a $5.5 million seed round led by Tower Research Ventures. The open-source project captures full coding sessions from more than 20 AI agents, distills them into reusable skills, and lets you switch tools without losing context.
It runs locally by default. X News says developers are praising it as a fix for repeated agent onboarding, with quick traction on GitHub as multi-agent workflows become normal.
